Maddeler şöyle yansıtılmaktadır: Gesichtsverhüllung (Yüz örtme) Alkoholverbot (Alkol yasağı), Weihnachten (fast) weg, (Noel neredeyse yok oldu) Befehlsgesellschaft 5 (Emir toplumu), Körperstrafe (Beden cezası), Verbot unzüchtigen Treffen (Ahlaksız buluşmaların yasaklanması). Enflasyonun hanehalkı eğlence ve kültür harcamaları üzerindeki etkisinin sınırlı olduğu bulgusuna rağmen, fiyat istikrarının korunması hanehalkı refahı açısından önemlidir. Ancak, enflasyonun hanehalkı eğlence ve kültür harcamaları üzerindeki etkisinin ihmal edilebilir düzeyde olması, bu alanda aşırı müdahaleci politikalardan kaçınılması gerektiğini göstermektedir. Bunun yerine, enflasyon hedeflemesi gibi ölçülü ve sürdürülebilir politikalar benimsenmelidir. Fiyat istikrarını sağlayabilmek açısından, eğlence ve kültür sektörünün sektörünün fiyat değişimlerinin izlenebilmesi için bir endeks oluşturabileceği düşünülmektedir.

unmatched_grobid.raw_reference: Enflasyonun hanehalkı eğlence ve kültür harcamaları üzerindeki etkisinin sınırlı olduğu bulgusuna rağmen, fiyat istikrarının korunması hanehalkı refahı açısından önemlidir. Ancak, enflasyonun hanehalkı eğlence ve kültür harcamaları üzerindeki etkisinin ihmal edilebilir düzeyde olması, bu alanda aşırı müdahaleci politikalardan kaçınılması gerektiğini göstermektedir. Bunun yerine, enflasyon hedeflemesi gibi ölçülü ve sürdürülebilir politikalar benimsenmelidir. Fiyat istikrarını sağlayabilmek açısından, eğlence ve kültür sektörünün sektörünün fiyat değişimlerinin izlenebilmesi için bir endeks oluşturabileceği düşünülmektedir.

references.raw_reference: Metal Lamp Components: Metal components were important complements in the use of glass lamps. They were used together with wick holders during the burning phase of the lamps and with metal lamp hang- ers and polycandelons for hanging the lamps. No polycandelon or fragments have yet been found among the metal finds from Olympos. However, the excavations revealed a large num- ber of oil lamp hangers, hooks, wick carriers and their fragments. Two oil lamp holders (cat. nos. 2.1.1., 2.1.2.), two wick carriers (cat. nos. 2.4.1., 2.4.2., 2.4.3.) and an oil lamp holder (cat. no. 2.5.1.) were recovered intact. In accordance with the catalog order, they can be listed as follows: 1.1. Lamp Hangers: From the early Byzantine period, they are known to have been used for hanging glass lamps. The pieces with cat. no. 2.1.1.1. and cat. no. 2.1.2. were produced by the casting technique. Cat. no. 2.1.1 consists of three separate hangers, the end of which is probably connected to a ring formed by bending it into a hook, as in the other example. At the end of each ring-shaped strap there are hooks that were hammered into shape. The hangers and hooks on cat. no. 40 Isings 1957, 162.

Metal Lamp Components: Metal components were important complements in the use of glass lamps. They were used together with wick holders during the burning phase of the lamps and with metal lamp hang- ers and polycandelons for hanging the lamps. No polycandelon or fragments have yet been found among the metal finds from Olympos. However, the excavations revealed a large num- ber of oil lamp hangers, hooks, wick carriers and their fragments. Two oil lamp holders (cat. nos. 2.1.1., 2.1.2.), two wick carriers (cat. nos. 2.4.1., 2.4.2., 2.4.3.) and an oil lamp holder (cat. no. 2.5.1.) were recovered intact. In accordance with the catalog order, they can be listed as follows: 1.1. Lamp Hangers: From the early Byzantine period, they are known to have been used for hanging glass lamps. The pieces with cat. no. 2.1.1.1. and cat. no. 2.1.2. were produced by the casting technique. Cat. no. 2.1.1 consists of three separate hangers, the end of which is probably connected to a ring formed by bending it into a hook, as in the other example. At the end of each ring-shaped strap there are hooks that were hammered into shape. The hangers and hooks on cat. no. 40 Isings 1957, 162.

Bossed blocks having a surface projecting directly from the joints are categorized into three types: 1) "quarry face" obtained from the quarry, 2) "hammer face" with some working with a hammer, 3) "pulvinated face" which exhib- its fine workmanship. All edges start with the same curvature culminating in a pillow-like boss in the center; see Scranton 1941, 22, 24, 107. For other studies and definitions, see Fyfe 1936, 120; Orlandos 1968, 162, 171; Ginouves and Martin 1985, 130; Müller-Wiener 1988, 73; Saner 1995, 32; Durukan 2004, 44.

Gate plans have two types from the beginning: An opening in the wall (axial) or two stretches of walls creating a corridor in between (overlapping). Axial gates are called Type 1 while overlapping gates are called Type 2; see Winter 1971, 208. For the overlap type, see Lawrence 1979, 306. See also McNicholl 1997, 6-7; Adam 1982, 77; Akarca 1998, 151; Frederiksen 2011, 55.

Gate plans have two types from the beginning: An opening in the wall (axial) or two stretches of walls creating a corridor in between (overlapping). Axial gates are called Type 1 while overlapping gates are called Type 2; see Winter 1971, 208. For the overlap type, see Lawrence 1979, 306. See also McNicholl 1997, 6-7; Adam 1982, 77; Akarca 1998, 151; Frederiksen 2011, 55.
Vitruvius writes that the ways leading to the gates should extend from the left, thus exposing the unprotected right- hand side of the troops (Vitr. De arch. I.5.2).
Passages in fortifications designed as courtyards or corridors to decrease the number of troops is known since the beginning of the Iron age. For examples of the early period, see Baran 2017, 123-24.
Akarca, on the other hand, categorizes these gates as gates with double towers, gates with towers and under-pas- sages, and gates with courtyards (Akarca 1998, 153-55).

In the high relief above the inscription, an equestrian dressed in a cloak and tunic is advancing toward an altar entwined by a serpent with a tree beside it. To the right of the altar stands a female figure, possibly in mourning, while at her feet an infant lies in a cradle. The stele is today in the Louvre Museum in Paris. Although a record from the Louvre Museum in 1901 states that this artifact originated from Sardis, L. references.raw_reference: From which source the inspiration came to the mind of the painter of the sarcophagus is another field arousing curiosity. At first glance, it may be assumed that the painter had seen an image similar to his painting, as suggested by the reference to Aeschylus' Eumenides mentioned above, or that he was influenced by a theatrical version in which the Boreads did not require wings. It is wellknown that many Attic vase paintings also existed bearing theatrical versions of the various myths, including the themes of Phineus, Harpies, and the Boreads. On the Attic redfigure amphora mentioned above (British Museum 1884.1007.82), Phineus is wearing a mask. See Padgett 1991, 2021, fig. 6; Green and Handly 1995, 41. However, as for the reasons behind such deviations in Ionian art, it has been suggested that Ionian painters of pottery and sarcophagi may have possessed knowledge of details from epic and lyric poetry, and that they occasionally incorporated these elements, even when such details were absent from Attic pottery. See Tempesta 1998, 31, 132, 136.

references.raw_reference: Within the framework of Ionian painting, some examples of such deviations exist that allow for a deeper discus- sion. For instance, Heracles is seen without his usual attributes or portrayed as a hoplite; some mythological crea- tures, such as Triton and Silenus, can be distinguished from their more familiar depictions by certain features and Priamus joins the scene of the ambush of Troilus on a sarcophagus from Abdera (no. G.7A), in contrast to most representations of this theme on Attic pottery. For a detailed analysis of the subject, see Tempesta 1998, 33, 4647, 104, 108, 110. An example of a deviation from the wellknown narrative scheme can be seen in Fikellura pottery. See Schlotzhauer 2024, 30. For a discussion on how Ionian artists may have interpreted familiar myths in a distinc- tive manner by synthesizing them with new elements from various sources due to Ionia's "borderland" position see Rodriguez 2025, 31114. Despite the brief overview presented above, Attic vase painting may still be considered 45 Cook 1981, 131; Kirchner 1987, 12829; Papalexandrou 2010, 1718.

For an extensive list of mythological subjects on Ionian pottery painting, see especially Tempesta 1998, 13176; Lemos 1991, 1078. Mythological themes in Ionian art other than pottery painting are beyond the scope of this article. However, for examples, the follow- ing may be consulted: Bronze relief from Samos depicting the fight between Heracles and Geryon, see Tsakos and ViglakiSofianau 2012, 15463. Ephesus Artemision reliefs illustrating Centauromachy, Gigantomachy, and Potnia Theron, see Muss 1994, 7988. Regarding mythological themes, the following examples may be considered in the context of Western Anatolia beyond Ionia: The subjects of Zeus with Europa, Heracles' fights with Pholos and Triton, and themes within the Trojan circle are depicted in the friezes of the Tempel of Athena at Assos. For detailed discussion of the mythological themes on the Tempel of Athena at Assos see esp. Wescoat 2012, 12791; Baykan 2016. Boston, Museum of Fine Arts, Inv. no. 84.67. From which source the inspiration came to the mind of the painter of the sarcophagus is another field arousing curiosity. At first glance, it may be assumed that the painter had seen an image similar to his painting, as suggested by the reference to Aeschylus' Eumenides mentioned above, or that he was influenced by a theatrical version in which the Boreads did not require wings. It is wellknown that many Attic vase paintings also existed bearing theatrical versions of the various myths, including the themes of Phineus, Harpies, and the Boreads. On the Attic redfigure amphora mentioned above (British Museum 1884.1007.82), Phineus is wearing a mask. See Padgett 1991, 2021, fig. 6; Green and Handly 1995, 41. However, as for the reasons behind such deviations in Ionian art, it has been suggested that Ionian painters of pottery and sarcophagi may have possessed knowledge of details from epic and lyric poetry, and that they occasionally incorporated these elements, even when such details were absent from Attic pottery. See Tempesta 1998, 31, 132, 136.

Within the framework of Ionian painting, some examples of such deviations exist that allow for a deeper discus- sion. For instance, Heracles is seen without his usual attributes or portrayed as a hoplite; some mythological crea- tures, such as Triton and Silenus, can be distinguished from their more familiar depictions by certain features and Priamus joins the scene of the ambush of Troilus on a sarcophagus from Abdera (no. G.7A), in contrast to most representations of this theme on Attic pottery. For a detailed analysis of the subject, see Tempesta 1998, 33, 4647, 104, 108, 110. An example of a deviation from the wellknown narrative scheme can be seen in Fikellura pottery. See Schlotzhauer 2024, 30. For a discussion on how Ionian artists may have interpreted familiar myths in a distinc- tive manner by synthesizing them with new elements from various sources due to Ionia's "borderland" position see Rodriguez 2025, 31114. Regarding mythological themes, the following examples may be considered in the context of Western Anatolia beyond Ionia: The subjects of Zeus with Europa, Heracles' fights with Pholos and Triton, and themes within the Trojan circle are depicted in the friezes of the Tempel of Athena at Assos. references.raw_reference: A single sherd of African Red Slip Ware was discovered among the finds of Boyalıtepe Höyük. According to Hayes' classification in his 1972 publication, the sherd belongs to form 3c. Hayes' form 3c represents plates with broad convex rims, shallow bodies, and low ring bases. Plates of Hayes' form 3 are often decorated with barbotine leaves on the rim. This form is divided into three subtypes. Hayes' form 3a and 3b bear decorations, whereas form 3c is undecorat- ed. 140 The sherd from Boyalıtepe Höyük is a small fragment, preserving only a small portion of rim and body. The broad convex rim is undecorated, aligning it with Hayes' form 3c.

African Red Slip Ware (cat. no. 47, fig. 12)

A single sherd of African Red Slip Ware was discovered among the finds of Boyalıtepe Höyük. According to Hayes' classification in his 1972 publication, the sherd belongs to form 3c. Hayes' form 3c represents plates with broad convex rims, shallow bodies, and low ring bases. Plates of Hayes' form 3 are often decorated with barbotine leaves on the rim. This form is divided into three subtypes. Hayes' form 3a and 3b bear decorations, whereas form 3c is undecorat- ed. 140 The sherd from Boyalıtepe Höyük is a small fragment, preserving only a small portion of rim and body. The broad convex rim is undecorated, aligning it with Hayes' form 3c.

These stelae can be observed in various locations within Yalvaç District, where the Hoyran and Sağır tombs are also situated at its boundaries; see Mitchell and Waelkens 1998, 8. fig. 4.1) Bowl with d=11 cm. Straight flaring walls and simple rim. Medium fine gray fab- ric with small grit, lime, much mica. Thick self-slip, badly worn off.

fig. 4.2) Bowl with d=15 cm. Straight flaring walls and simple rim. Coarse buff fabric with much grit, lime, and little mica, also organic inclusions. Surface color varies from buff to reddish buff creating a mottled effect due to uneven firing. Self-slipped, smoothed / low burnished.
fig. 4.3) Bowl with d=16 cm. Straight flaring walls and simple rim. Fabric and surface treatment like nr. 2, but surface more evenly fired. Surface badly worn-off.
fig. 4.4) Bowl with d=17 cm. Straight flaring walls and simple rim. Fabric and surface treatment like nr. 2 but overall better fired.
fig. 4.5) Bowl with d=17 cm. Straight flaring walls and simple rim. Medium fine buff fabric with small grit, lime, and little mica. Self-slipped, low-burnished. Well fired. No dark core.
fig. 4.6) Bowl with d=26 cm. Slightly incurving walls and simple rim. Fabric and surface treatment like nr. 2. Surface badly worn-off.

fig. 4.7) Bowl with d=50 cm. Slightly incurving walls and simple rim. Outside three verti- cal grooves from rim preserved. Fabric coarse with much large grit, lime, and little mica, copious organic inclusions. Surface not treated showing details of inclusions especially burned off organic inclusions.
fig. 4.8) Bowl with d=43 cm. Slightly incurving walls and simple rim. Vertical loop han- dle. Coarse buff fabric with much grit, lime, and little mica, also organic inclusions. Slip badly worn-off.

fig. 4.9) Hemispherical bowl with d=8 cm. Simple rim. Outside 2 chevron-shaped grooves preserved. Medium coarse buff fabric with much grit, lime, and little mica, also organic inclusions. Self-slipped. Outside slip worn-off, not clear if burnished. Inside smoothed. Better fired, no dark core.
fig. 4.10) Hemispherical bowl with d=16 cm. Simple rim. Fabric and surface treatment like nr. 2.
fig. 4.11) Hemispherical bowl with d=18 cm. Simple rim. Fabric and surface treatment like nr. 9.

fig. 4.12) Hemispherical bowl with d=21 cm. Simple rim. Coarse buff fabric with much grit, lime, and little mica, also organic inclusions. Thick self-slip, medium burnished. Slip worn-off outside, cracked inside. Color variation due to uneven firing creating a mottled effect.

fig. 4.13) Hemispherical bowl with d=19 cm. Simple rim. Outside three vertical grooves from rim preserved. Coarse buff fabric with much grit, lime, and little mica, also organic inclusions. Outside and inside rim area black probably due to stacking during firing.

fig. 5.11) Pithos fragment. Ten fingerprint impressions, one a bit further and impressed larger. Also, two horn-like protrusions, one only preserved partially. Fabric and surface treatment like nr. 27.

fig. 4.14) Hemispherical bowl with d=28 cm. Simple rim. Wide vertical loop handle with three ridges, two along the sides and one in the middle. Coarse fabric with much grit, lime, and little mica, also organic inclusions. Thick self-slip, medium burnished. Slip cracked inside. Color variation due to uneven firing.
fig. 4.15) Hemispherical bowl with d=21 cm. Simple rim. Oversized vertical handle with wide horizontal oblique ridges creating a twisted visual effect. Fabric and surface treat- ment like nr. 7.
fig. 4.16) Hemispherical shallow bowl with d=41 cm. Simple rim. Horizontal loop handle. Fabric and surface treatment like nr. 2.
fig. 4.17) Hemispherical bowl with d=47 cm. Simple rim. Horizontal loop handle. Fabric and surface treatment like nr. 2.
fig. 4.18) Hemispherical bowl with d=54 cm. Simple rim. Horizontal loop handle. Fabric and surface treatment like nr. 2.
fig. 5.1) Hole mouth pot with d=22 cm. Simple rim. Three vertical grooves from rim pre- served. Fabric and surface treatment like nr. 2.

fig. 5.2) Small jar / multiple cup with everted rim d=4 cm. Joint mark on the shoulder. Medium coarse clay with little grit (some brown) lime, some mica. Self-slipped. Outside burnished. Better fired.
fig. 5.3) Small jar / multiple cup with everted rim d=7 cm. Joint mark on the shoulder. Medium coarse clay, like nr. 20, but less coarse. Outside and rim area very low burnished.
fig. 5.4) Jar with everted rim d=10 cm. Rising handle from the rim. Fabric and surface treatment like nr. 12.
fig. 5.5) Jar or pedestal base with d=5 cm. Medium black fabric with small to medium grit, little lime, and much mica. Self-slipped, medium burnished. Fabric not local and of higher quality.
fig. 5.6) Jar with flattened rim d=56 cm. Coarse buff fabric with much grit, lime, and little mica, also organic inclusions. Self-slipped and smoothed.

fig. 5.7) Wide handle with three vertical grooves. Coarse buff fabric with much grit, lime, and little mica, also organic inclusions. Thick self-slipped, medium burnished. Side facing inside not treated and dark in color, also black core.
fig. 5.8) Plug handle with oblique grooves creating the visual effect of twisted clay. Coarse fabric with much grit and lime (some very large), little mica. Surface badly worn-off.

fig. 5.9) Pithos fragment. Two mammiform bosses preserved. Very coarse heavy fabric with copious grit and lime (some very large) and little mica. Also, much organic inclu- sions. Self-slipped. Surface badly worn-off.
fig. 5.10) Pithos fragment. Two mammiform bosses preserved. Fabric and surface treat- ment like nr. 27.

references.raw_reference: Es handelt sich um Avcu und Uzunoğlu 2024, 202-4, nr. 8 (s. schon Linnemann 2013, 141, n. 1852 u.ö.). Der Text lautet: θήκη διαφέρουσα Θεωδώρου διακόνου μονῖς τοῦ ἁγίου Σεργίου καὶ Κόνονος. Bei strenger grammatischer Auslegung wäre wegen des Singulars τοῦ ἁγίου davon auszugehen, dass das Kloster nur Sergios geweiht ist und Konon eine weitere bestattete Person ist. Ein Heiligen-Paar "Sergios und Konon" ist auch anderweitig nicht be- kannt. Das καὶ Κόνονος scheint jedoch keine spätere Ergänzung zu sein.

Beispiele wären: Dindebol (Dometiopolis), Yukarı İzvit (Sbide), İznebol (Zenonopolis), Lavşa (Lauzadeai) oder Muzvadı (Mousbada), vgl. Pilhofer 2018, 20.
Vgl. etwa Ruffing 2008, 769-71, s.v. ταριχᾶς bzw. ταριχοπώλης. Dazu s. auch die schwer zu interpretierende Inschrift Keil und Wilhelm 1931, nr. 408 mit der Buchstabenfolge ταριχίου (aus Korykos!).

Der Ortname müßte im Genitiv stehen. Die Endung -α ist zwar durchaus eine übliche einheimische Genitivendung, Laminger-Pascher 1973, 81 bietet eine ganze Liste mit vergleichbaren Fällen. Aber insgesamt wäre die Konstruktion aus Herkunft und Beruf eher ungewöhnlich.

Im Index von ETAM 22 finden sich 39 Belege, davon 30 aus Korykos. Für das kleinasiatische Inland bietet LGPN V.C, 389, acht Belege, ungefähr die Hälfte davon würden zeitlich passen. An der gesamten Südküste von Karien bis Kilikien hat LGPN V.B, 382, 36 Belege, die alle aus dem Rauhen Kilikien stammen.
Vgl. Keil und Wilhelm 1931, nr. 99.

ETAM 22 hat keinen Beleg. LGPN V.C Inland, 135, hat zwei Belege, einen galatischen aus byzantinischer Zeit und einen pisidischen aus der Kaiserzeit. Für die Südküste hat LGPN V.B, 133, vier Belege, die alle aus dem kaiserzeit- lichen Karien stammen.
Daher bemerkt LSJ s.v. πατριώτης pointiert: "prop. of barbarians who had only a common πατρίς, πολῖται being used of Greeks who had a common πόλις" (1349).

Historia Alexandri Magni, Rezension φ (= Veloudis 1977), 110.8: Ἀλέξανδρε βασιλεῦ, συμπατριῶτα, υἱὲ τοῦ Νεκτεναβοῦ βασιλέως, κάμε ἔλεος εἰς ἐμᾶς. Im Heiligenkult wird der Begriff auf Demetrios von Thessaloniki ange- wendet (Abschnitt 2 in Laourdas 1960).
Zu den Nachweisen vgl. LBG s.v. συμπατριώτης (1655).

Pilhofer 2020, 53.56. Für eine genaue Diskussion der Belege seiner Verehrung in der Kalykadnos-Region s. Pilhofer 2020, 43-56, für Kleinasien und darüber hinaus bis Ägypten und Rom s. dort S. 57-70. Zur Konstruktion der Region als lieu de mémoire s. Pilhofer 2021.

Es handelt sich um Avcu und Uzunoğlu 2024, 202-4, nr. 8 (s. schon Linnemann 2013, 141, n. 1852 u.ö.). Der Text lautet: θήκη διαφέρουσα Θεωδώρου διακόνου μονῖς τοῦ ἁγίου Σεργίου καὶ Κόνονος. Bei strenger grammatischer Auslegung wäre wegen des Singulars τοῦ ἁγίου davon auszugehen, dass das Kloster nur Sergios geweiht ist und Konon eine weitere bestattete Person ist. Ein Heiligen-Paar "Sergios und Konon" ist auch anderweitig nicht be- kannt. Das καὶ Κόνονος scheint jedoch keine spätere Ergänzung zu sein.
Dazu vgl. Kollmann 2021, 21-46, gerade zur Kalykadnos-Region s. auch Pilhofer 2018, 205-29.
Die spätantiken Thekla-Wunder berichten davon, dass der Metropolit zweimal täglich psalmodierend in ihr Heiligtum gepilgert sei: VMTh II 44, 26-32 (Dagron 1978).
Die Inschrift ist überliefert durch Hicks 1891, 261, nr. 38 (= ETAM 22, Lam 14); zu den inhaltlichen Aspekten s. Pilhofer 2018, 250-51.

VMTh II 24 Das Kind verlor ein Augenlicht. Geheilt wurde es im Vorhof der Thekla-Kirche in Ayatekla durch einen Kranich, der in ebendieses Auge pickte (Übersetzung Schröder): Das "erregte in der Stadt [Olba] sowie beim Vater und dem Großvater großes Erstaunen. Ersterer heißt Pardamios, der Großvater aber heißt Anatolios, er ist auch Priester der dortigen Kirche."

Due to the early occurrence of Samian amphorae in Phoenician settlements such as Carthage and Toscanos, the traditional view that Samian amphorae were first produced in the late 7th or early 6th century BC requires revision. According to the latest data, the production of Samian amphorae begins at the end of 8th century BCE. Knidian amphorae have a distinctive form from the end of the 4th century BCE onwards. The amphorae type has a rounded, everted rim, long conical neck, oval-sectioned vertical handles, and ovoid body tapering to a plastic ring attached to conical spike; see Şenol 2003, 35. The amphorae group called Zenon A are dated to 280-275 BCE due to their discovery in the Serçe Limanı Shipwreck and their stamps; see Grace 1986, 554, 561. 70 Empereur and Hesnard 1987, 59; Tuna and Empereur 1988, 345.

references.raw_reference: The invention of glass blowing, the production model that began in the Roman period, has almost always been described as a 'revolution' in the literature. This is because glass blowing, invented in the first century BC, en- abled glass to be produced more cheaply, efficiently, and quickly than had previously been possible. In fact, by the end of the first century AD, glass had become a common household item in areas dominated by the Roman empire. See Larson 2016.

John Chrysostom probably wrote his treatise on Babylas between the years 363 and 380. His mention in the text of a peace treaty with the Persians on the death of the Roman emperor Julian the Apostate implies a date after 363. 58 The absence of any mention of the martyrion built by Meletius, bishop of Antioch, across the Orontes River in 379-380 indicates that the trea- tise was written before this date. Chrysostom said that Gallus was inspired by God, who had mercy on the inhabitants of the region because of the immorality of the youths in the temple of Apollo. 59 It is clearly understood that Chrysostom interpreted the martyrdom of Babylas in terms of the triumph of Christianity over paganism. In this way, the cult of Apollo, a Greek god 53 Chronique de Séert, 1.2, 72.

'tür. Hedef kitle kimlerdir sorusuna verilen yanıtların sayısı 3, oyunun kazanımları nelerdir ve neler öğrendik soruları ise her biri için 2 katılımcı tarafından cevaplanmıştır. Katılımcıların görüşleri ise şu şekildedir: K1: "Kendi projemden söyleyeyim. Kendi oyunumda ne görmek isterim diye düşünürsem şey olabilir. Mesela nasıl oynanır, içeriği nedir, oyunda neler kullanıldı. Bunları yapabilirim. Oyunun kazanımı nedir gibi." K2: "Uygulamanın amacı, uygulama içerikleri (bölüm bölüm uygulamayı tanıtma) uygulama örneklerine yer verilebilir." K4: "Kullanım kılavuzu için oyun nasıl oynanır, bu oyunda neleri hedefliyoruz, amacımız nedir. Öğrendikten sonra neleri yapabiliriz. Mesela matematikte işlemleri öğrendikten sonar gerçek hayatta nasıl kullanabiliriz gibi." K5: "Nasıl oynanır? Neler öğrendim? Neler öğreneceğiz?" K6: "Bu programı niçin kullanıyoruz? Ne amaçla kullanıyoruz, hem öğrenen için daha hızlı öğrenmeler sağlanır. Hedef kitleye uygunluk ve yazı ve görsel kullanımı uygun olmalıdır. Programda neler kullanacağız neler yapabiliriz? Şeklinde olacaktır." K7: "En başta dikkat çeksin diye eğlenerek öğreniyorum derdim. İçeriğini ne anlatacaksam eğlenceli olarak belirlerdim. Konu başlığını dikkat çekici seçerdim. Oyun geliştirmenin kullanılabileceği alanlar nelerdir olabilir? Hangi seviyeye hangi uygulamaların kullanılacağı başlığı olabilir." K8: "Yapacağım oyun ile ilgili bir başlık seçerdim. Tabi ki hedef belirleriz…Oyunun nasıl oynanacağı nasıl yazıldığı ve kurulduğu gibi açıklamak zorunda kalırdık. Nereden nereye nasıl ulaşabiliriz. Hangi sayfalarda hangi içerikler var? Şeklinde yaparım." K10: "Oyun tabanlı öğrenme nedir? Oyun tabanlı öğrenme nasıl uygulanır? Kazanımlar" Katılımcıların görüşlerinin ortak bir noktası, oyun tabanlı öğrenme uygulamalarında yer alacak başlıkların, içerik ile uyumlu olması gerektiğidir. Oyun tabanlı öğrenme uygulamaları için katılımcılardan gelen başlık önerileri arasında "Neler öğrendim?", "Kazanımlar nelerdir?", "Uygulamanın amacı nedir?" gibi ifadeler yer almıştır. Bu başlıkların, uygulamanın içeriğini etkili bir biçimde yansıtacağı düşünülmektedir. Ayrıca, içeriğin değerlendirilmesi ve amaçlarına yönelik görüşlere de yer verilmiştir. Oyun tabanlı öğrenme uygulamalarıyla ilgili başlıkların katılımcılar tarafından nasıl değerlendirildiği, Şekil 1'de gösterilmektedir. Hedef kitle kimlerdir sorusuna verilen yanıtların sayısı 3, oyunun kazanımları nelerdir ve neler öğrendik soruları ise her biri için 2 katılımcı tarafından cevaplanmıştır. Katılımcıların görüşleri ise şu şekildedir: K1: "Kendi projemden söyleyeyim. Kendi oyunumda ne görmek isterim diye düşünürsem şey olabilir. Mesela nasıl oynanır, içeriği nedir, oyunda neler kullanıldı. Bunları yapabilirim. Oyunun kazanımı nedir gibi." K2: "Uygulamanın amacı, uygulama içerikleri (bölüm bölüm uygulamayı tanıtma) uygulama örneklerine yer verilebilir." K4: "Kullanım kılavuzu için oyun nasıl oynanır, bu oyunda neleri hedefliyoruz, amacımız nedir. Öğrendikten sonra neleri yapabiliriz. Mesela matematikte işlemleri öğrendikten sonar gerçek hayatta nasıl kullanabiliriz gibi." K5: "Nasıl oynanır? Neler öğrendim? Neler öğreneceğiz?" K6: "Bu programı niçin kullanıyoruz? Ne amaçla kullanıyoruz, hem öğrenen için daha hızlı öğrenmeler sağlanır. Hedef kitleye uygunluk ve yazı ve görsel kullanımı uygun olmalıdır. Programda neler kullanacağız neler yapabiliriz? Şeklinde olacaktır." K7: "En başta dikkat çeksin diye eğlenerek öğreniyorum derdim. İçeriğini ne anlatacaksam eğlenceli olarak belirlerdim. Konu başlığını dikkat çekici seçerdim. Oyun geliştirmenin kullanılabileceği alanlar nelerdir olabilir? Hangi seviyeye hangi uygulamaların kullanılacağı başlığı olabilir." K8: "Yapacağım oyun ile ilgili bir başlık seçerdim. Tabi ki hedef belirleriz…Oyunun nasıl oynanacağı nasıl yazıldığı ve kurulduğu gibi açıklamak zorunda kalırdık. Nereden nereye nasıl ulaşabiliriz. Hangi sayfalarda hangi içerikler var? Şeklinde yaparım." K10: "Oyun tabanlı öğrenme nedir? Oyun tabanlı öğrenme nasıl uygulanır? Kazanımlar" Katılımcıların görüşlerinin ortak bir noktası, oyun tabanlı öğrenme uygulamalarında yer alacak başlıkların, içerik ile uyumlu olması gerektiğidir. Oyun tabanlı öğrenme uygulamaları için katılımcılardan gelen başlık önerileri arasında "Neler öğrendim?", "Kazanımlar nelerdir?", "Uygulamanın amacı nedir?" gibi ifadeler yer almıştır. Bu başlıkların, uygulamanın içeriğini etkili bir biçimde yansıtacağı düşünülmektedir. Ayrıca, içeriğin değerlendirilmesi ve amaçlarına yönelik görüşlere de yer verilmiştir. Oyun tabanlı öğrenme uygulamalarıyla ilgili başlıkların katılımcılar tarafından nasıl değerlendirildiği, Şekil 1'de gösterilmektedir. sonra Osmanlı düşüncesinin ilerleyen safhalarına bunların hangi imkân ve sorunları getirdiğinin tespiti ise kitabı okuyan araştırmaların uhdesine düşüyor. Sonuç olarak Molla Lutfi Fütûhât'ı, bir "meseleler kitabı" gibi işliyor. Özellikle umûr-ı âmme (genel ilkeler), kelâm ilminin mevzuu, mecʿûliyet, hudûs (yaratılmışlık), nefsü'l-emr, Allah'ın sıfatları, fiilleri ve diğer önemli meseleleri çözümlemeye çalışıyor. Bu meseleler, hem İbn Sînâ sonrası felsefe-kelâm tartışmalarının Osmanlı'da nasıl sürdüğünü, hem de II. Bayezid dönemi entelektüel ikliminde hangi konuların öncelikli olduğunu çok net gösteriyor.
